claims.claim: The levels of Kip2-S63A-3xsfGFP linearly increase from the minus- to the plus-ends of the microtubules.
claims.source: In contrast, the distribution profile of Kip2-S63A-3xsfGFP along microtubules deviated strongly from that of Kip2-3xsfGFP and resembled more that of Kip3 (Figure 1a): The levels of Kip2-S63A-3xsfGFP linearly increased from the minus- to the plus-ends of the microtubules, and plus-end levels increased with microtubule length (Figure 6f, Video 3).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by line scanning analysis shown in Figure 6f.

claims.claim: Plus-end levels of Kip2-S63A-3xsfGFP increase with microtubule length.
claims.source: In contrast, the distribution profile of Kip2-S63A-3xsfGFP along microtubules deviated strongly from that of Kip2-3xsfGFP and resembled more that of Kip3 (Figure 1a): The levels of Kip2-S63A-3xsfGFP linearly increased from the minus- to the plus-ends of the microtubules, and plus-end levels increased with microtubule length (Figure 6f, Video 3).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by line scanning analysis shown in Figure 6f.

claims.claim: The median on-rate constant of Kip2-S63A (kon) is significantly higher than for the wild type protein.
claims.source: These estimates indicate that the median on-rate constant of Kip2-S63A (kon) is significantly higher than for the wild type protein (p<2∙10−4 when assuming a Kip2 concentration of ≥ 35 nM, Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3abd, see Supplemental information for details), while the median in-rate constant (kin, minus-end recruitment) is not significantly changed (Figure 6g).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by mathematical modeling shown in Figure 6g.

claims.claim: The median in-rate constant (kin, minus-end recruitment) is not significantly changed in Kip2-S63A.
claims.source: These estimates indicate that the median on-rate constant of Kip2-S63A (kon) is significantly higher than for the wild type protein (p<2∙10−4 when assuming a Kip2 concentration of ≥ 35 nM, Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3abd, see Supplemental information for details), while the median in-rate constant (kin, minus-end recruitment) is not significantly changed (Figure 6g).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by mathematical modeling shown in Figure 6g.

claims.claim: Phosphorylation of Kip2's N-terminus primarily inhibits Kip2 from landing on microtubules.
claims.source: These estimates indicate that phosphorylation of Kip2's N-terminus primarily inhibits Kip2 from landing on microtubules.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results showing increased on-rate in Kip2-S63A.

claims.claim: The hypo-phosphorylated, ATPase-deficient Kip2-S63A-G374A-3xsfGFP protein decorates both microtubule shafts and SPBs in heterozygous diploid cells co-expressing Kip2-mCherry.
claims.source: Consistent with this hypothesis, the hypo-phosphorylated, ATPase-deficient Kip2-S63A-G374A-3xsfGFP protein decorated both microtubule shafts and SPBs in heterozygous diploid cells co-expressing Kip2-mCherry (Figure 6hi).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by imaging shown in Figure 6h-i.

claims.claim: The Kip2-S63A mutation largely bypasses the differential control of Kip2 recruitment to microtubules exerted by SPBs.
claims.source: Furthermore, the Kip2-S63A mutation largely bypassed the differential control of Kip2 recruitment to microtubules exerted by SPBs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that Kip2-S63A shows more symmetric distribution.

claims.claim: The levels of Kip2-S63A-3xsfGFP on plus-ends increase on both m- and b-microtubules.
claims.source: The levels of Kip2-S63A-3xsfGFP on plus-ends increased on both m- and b-microtubules, and the level differences between them were substantially reduced compared to wild type (Figure 6j and Figure 4e).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 6j.

claims.claim: The level differences of Kip2-S63A-3xsfGFP between m- and b-microtubules are substantially reduced compared to wild type.
claims.source: The levels of Kip2-S63A-3xsfGFP on plus-ends increased on both m- and b-microtubules, and the level differences between them were substantially reduced compared to wild type (Figure 6j and Figure 4e).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 6j.

claims.claim: The asymmetry of hypo-phosphorylated Kip2-S63A-3xsfGFP levels between m- and b-microtubule plus-ends is reduced and no-longer depends on whether the spindle is properly oriented or not.
claims.source: Moreover, the asymmetry of hypo-phosphorylated Kip2-S63A-3xsfGFP levels between m- and b-microtubule plus-ends was reduced and no-longer depended on whether the spindle was properly oriented or not (Figure 6k and Figure 4f).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by asymmetry index quantification shown in Figure 6k.

claims.claim: Preventing Kip2 landing along microtubules is a pre-requisite for the control of Kip2 recruitment by SPBs.
claims.source: Therefore, preventing Kip2 landing along microtubules is a pre-requisite for the control of Kip2 recruitment by SPBs and Kip2 phosphorylation is key in this process.

claims.claim: Kip2 phosphorylation is key in preventing Kip2 landing along microtubules.
claims.source: Therefore, preventing Kip2 landing along microtubules is a pre-requisite for the control of Kip2 recruitment by SPBs and Kip2 phosphorylation is key in this process.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the effects of the Kip2-S63A mutation.

claims.claim: Neither Kip2 phosphorylation nor Bub2 and Bfa1 control the differential rate of microtubule nucleation between m- and b-SPBs by themselves.

claims.claim: Kip2 hypo-phosphorylation (KIP2-S63A mutant cells) causes both m- and b-microtubules to become longer on average compared to wild type cells.
claims.source: Kip2 hypo-phosphorylation (KIP2-S63A mutant cells) caused both m- and b-microtubules to become longer on average compared to wild type cells (Figure 7ab), in agreement with these microtubules carrying higher levels of the microtubule polymerizing kinesin Kip2 at their plus-ends (Figure 6j and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by microtubule length measurements shown in Figure 7a-b.

claims.claim: In KIP2-S63A mutant cells, the m- and b-microtubules are no-longer significantly different in length.
claims.source: In these mutant cells, the m- and b-microtubules were no-longer significantly different in length.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by microtubule length measurements shown in Figure 7b.

claims.claim: Inactivation of Bfa1, Bub2, or both eliminates the length difference between m- and b-microtubules by reducing the average length of b- to that of m-microtubules.
claims.source: Inactivation of Bfa1, Bub2, or both also eliminated the length difference between m- and b-microtubules, but in this case by reducing the average length of b- to that of m-microtubules (Figure 7ab).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by microtubule length measurements shown in Figure 7a-b.

claims.claim: The KIP2-S63A, bfa1∆, bub2∆, and bfa1∆ bub2∆ mutations randomize dynein distribution in cells carrying both b- and m- microtubules.
claims.source: Consistent with these effects, the KIP2-S63A, bfa1∆, bub2∆, and bfa1∆ bub2∆ mutations randomized dynein distribution in cells carrying both b- and m- microtubules (Figure 7cd).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by dynein localization and asymmetry quantification shown in Figure 7c-d.

claims.claim: In KIP2-S63A, bfa1∆, bub2∆, and bfa1∆ bub2∆ mutant cells, Dyn1-mNeonGreen localizes indistinguishably to the tip of both b- and m-microtubules.

claims.evidence: Demonstrated by dynein localization shown in Figure 7c-d.

claims.claim: Restricting the initiation of Kip2 runs to the b-SPBs functions as a molecular determinant for specifying the length and function of b-microtubules in vivo.
claims.source: We therefore concluded that restricting the initiation of Kip2 runs to the b-SPBs functioned as a molecular determinant for specifying the length and function of b-microtubules in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the effects of mutations affecting Kip2 recruitment on microtubule length and dynein distribution.

claims.claim: The remote-control mechanism for patterning microtubule organization and function relies on a dedicated mode of kinesin regulation.
claims.source: Here, we identify a remote-control mechanism for patterning microtubule organization and function at the subcellular level in yeast and demonstrate that this mechanism relies on a dedicated mode of kinesin regulation (Figure 7e).
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, summarized in Figure 7e.

claims.claim: The cytoplasmic pool of the kinesin is inhibited in its ability to bind microtubules at random positions.
claims.source: This process relies on two main conditions: the cytoplasmic pool of the kinesin is inhibited in its ability to bind microtubules at random positions, and at least one MTOC provides activities promoting the recruitment and reactivation of the kinesin locally, at the minus-end of the microtubule.
claims.evidence: This is a key finding demonstrated by the effects of Kip2 phosphorylation.

claims.claim: At least one MTOC provides activities promoting the recruitment and reactivation of the kinesin locally, at the minus-end of the microtubule.
claims.source: This process relies on two main conditions: the cytoplasmic pool of the kinesin is inhibited in its ability to bind microtubules at random positions, and at least one MTOC provides activities promoting the recruitment and reactivation of the kinesin locally, at the minus-end of the microtubule.
claims.evidence: This is a key finding demonstrated by the role of Bub2/Bfa1 and SPB-dependent recruitment.

claims.claim: Releasing the specificity of the SPB or the cytoplasmic inhibition of the kinesin equalizes the distribution of the kinesin and its cargoes, and prevents microtubule differentiation.
claims.source: Releasing the specificity of the SPB or the cytoplasmic inhibition of the kinesin equalizes the distribution of the kinesin and its cargoes, and prevents microtubule differentiation.

claims.claim: In budding yeast, the remote-control of microtubule plus-ends by the SPBs is a major mechanism for establishing spindle asymmetry and differentiating the behavior of selected microtubules.
claims.source: Thus, at least in budding yeast, the remote-control of microtubule plus-ends by the SPBs is a major mechanism for establishing spindle asymmetry and differentiating the behavior of selected microtubules.

claims.claim: Kip2 recruitment activity at SPBs most likely requires high-affinity or many low-affinity binding sites for phosphorylated Kip2 at the MTOC.
claims.source: As a consequence, Kip2 recruitment activity at SPBs most likely requires two components. First, a high-affinity or many low-affinity binding sites for phosphorylated Kip2 must be present at the MTOC to ensure its recruitment against competing binding sites on microtubules: even if phosphorylated Kip2 binds them only poorly, the surface of the microtubules in the cell and the number of tubulin dimers that they expose is orders of magnitude greater than the size of the microtubule minus-end.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference based on the need to compete with microtubule binding sites.

claims.evidence: This is a logical inference based on the need for Kip2 to bind microtubules to walk along them.

results.result: Yeast SPBs differentially control microtubule plus-end dynamics and cargo delivery through a remote-control mechanism. The old SPB recruits Kip2, which translocates to microtubule plus-ends, promotes extension, and delivers dynein to the bud, establishing spindle asymmetry.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 are well-supported by extensive experimental data including microscopy (Figures 3-4), quantitative analyses of Kip2 and dynein distribution, and functional assays. The mechanism (C11, C164, C168) is demonstrated through multiple complementary approaches including mutant analysis and mathematical modeling. The data consistently show asymmetric Kip2 recruitment and its functional consequences.

results.result: Kip3 functions as a length-dependent microtubule depolymerase in vivo, with intensity increasing linearly along microtubules and plus-end accumulation proportional to microtubule length.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C68 are supported by line scanning analysis (Figure 1a) and quantification showing linear increase in Kip3 intensity with distance and length. The conclusion is consistent with published in vitro data and the antenna model, providing strong convergent evidence.

results.result: Kip2 distribution in vivo differs from in vitro patterns, showing flat distribution along microtubules with a plus-end peak, independent of microtubule length, suggesting a distinct regulatory mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C72 are well-supported by line scanning analysis (Figure 1b) and technical replicates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d). The sharp contrast with in vitro data and Kip3 distribution provides strong evidence for a unique in vivo regulatory mechanism.

results.result: Mathematical modeling indicates Kip2 initiates runs predominantly from microtubule minus-ends, with the in-rate constant approximately 500 times higher than the on-rate constant at lattice sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C78 are supported by analytical and numerical modeling (Figure 2, Appendix 1) that faithfully reproduces experimental distributions. Parameter estimates match published values, and statistical significance (p<5×10⁻⁵) is demonstrated. The modeling provides strong quantitative support for minus-end recruitment.

results.result: Kip2 runs are initiated exclusively from SPBs and travel to microtubule plus-ends at 6.3 ± 2.1 µm min⁻¹, more than four times faster than microtubule growth speed.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C83, C86 are supported by kymograph analysis (Figure 3a, Video 1) and line scan analysis (Figure 3b) showing all unambiguous Kip2 speckles (n=192) originating from SPBs. Speed measurements are quantified with appropriate sample sizes. The conclusion is well-supported by direct observation.

results.result: ATPase-deficient Kip2-G374A accumulates exclusively at SPBs, specifically on the cytoplasmic side overlapping with Spc72, demonstrating that Kip2 recruitment is restricted to SPBs.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C92 are supported by localization experiments (Figure 3c, Figure 3—figure supplement 2) showing exclusive SPB localization of the non-motile mutant. Colocalization with SPB markers provides strong spatial evidence. The inference about recruitment restriction is well-justified.

results.result: In heterozygous diploid cells, Kip2-G374A remains at SPBs and is not transported to plus-ends by wild-type Kip2, demonstrating that Kip2 landing is restricted to SPBs and excluding direct plus-end recruitment.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C98 are supported by imaging of heterozygous diploid cells (Figure 3d) showing differential localization of wild-type and mutant proteins. The inference about heterodimer inactivity (C96) is reasonable given the data, though direct biochemical evidence would strengthen it. The conclusion about SPB-restricted landing is well-supported.

results.result: The two SPBs recruit different levels of Kip2, with b-SPBs accumulating approximately four times more than m-SPBs. Both SPB age and proximity to the bud neck synergistically activate Kip2 recruitment.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C107 are supported by quantification (Figure 4a-c) with large sample sizes (>1400 cells). The analysis of correctly oriented vs. inverted SPBs provides strong evidence for dual control by age and position. Statistical significance is demonstrated, and the synergistic effect is well-documented.

results.result: SPB-dependent Kip2 recruitment correlates with microtubule length differences and dynein distribution, with b-microtubules being twice as long and carrying more dynein than m-microtubules.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C116 are supported by quantification of Kip2 at plus-ends (Figure 4d-e), microtubule length measurements (Figure 4g), and dynein localization (Figure 4h-i). The correlations are well-documented with appropriate controls (kip2Δ, Kip2-G374A mutants). The mechanistic link is strongly supported.

results.result: Bub2 and Bfa1 contribute to Kip2 recruitment on b-SPBs. Their deletion reduces Kip2-G374A levels on b-SPBs by half and decreases the in-rate constant 12-fold without affecting the on-rate constant.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C131 are supported by quantification in mutants (Figure 5a-c) and mathematical modeling (Figure 5e, p=0.0008). The pattern of Kip2 distribution along microtubules remains unchanged (C128), supporting the specific effect on minus-end recruitment. The conclusion is well-supported by multiple lines of evidence.

results.result: In bfa1Δ and bub2Δ mutants, Kip2 levels at b-microtubule plus-ends drop to m-microtubule levels while m-microtubule levels remain unchanged, demonstrating that Bub2 and Bfa1 specifically enhance Kip2 recruitment on b-SPBs.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C135 are supported by quantification (Figure 5f-g) showing specific reduction in b-microtubule Kip2 levels. The asymmetry index analysis confirms equalization of distribution. The conclusion about specific b-SPB enhancement is well-justified by the data.

results.result: Kip2's N-terminus is heavily phosphorylated in vivo in a GSK3-, Cdk1-, and Dbf2/20-dependent manner, with GSK3 phosphorylation primed through serine 63. This phosphorylation inhibits Kip2 binding to microtubules.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C140 are supported by citations to established literature (Drechsler et al., 2015) and Western blot data (Figure 6b). The conservation of serine 63 is demonstrated by sequence alignment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). The functional consequence is well-established in the literature.

results.result: The Kip2-S63A mutation increases SPB recruitment but maintains asymmetry. However, the distribution along microtubules changes dramatically to resemble Kip3, with linear increase from minus to plus-ends and length-dependent accumulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C146 are supported by quantification (Figure 6c-e) and line scanning analysis (Figure 6f, Video 3). The differential effects on SPB recruitment vs. lattice binding provide strong evidence for the specific role of phosphorylation in preventing lattice binding.

results.result: Mathematical modeling shows that the Kip2-S63A mutation significantly increases the on-rate constant (p<2×10⁻⁴) without changing the in-rate constant, indicating that phosphorylation primarily inhibits lattice binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C149 are supported by mathematical modeling (Figure 6g) with statistical significance testing. The specific increase in on-rate without change in in-rate provides strong quantitative evidence for the mechanism. The conclusion is well-justified by the modeling results.

results.result: The Kip2-S63A mutation bypasses SPB control by allowing lattice binding, equalizing Kip2 distribution between m- and b-microtubules. This demonstrates that preventing lattice binding through phosphorylation is essential for SPB-dependent control.
results.evaluation: Claims C150-C156 are supported by imaging of heterozygous diploid cells (Figure 6h-i) and quantification (Figure 6j-k). The equalization of distribution and loss of orientation-dependence provide strong evidence. The conclusion about the requirement for phosphorylation is well-supported.

results.result: Mutations affecting Kip2 control (KIP2-S63A, bfa1Δ, bub2Δ) eliminate microtubule length differences and randomize dynein distribution, demonstrating that SPB-dependent Kip2 recruitment specifies b-microtubule length and function.
results.evaluation: Claims C158-C163 are supported by microtubule length measurements (Figure 7a-b) and dynein localization (Figure 7c-d). The complementary effects of different mutations (increasing vs. decreasing Kip2 levels) provide strong evidence for the causal relationship. The conclusion is well-justified.

results.result: The remote-control mechanism relies on two conditions: cytoplasmic inhibition of kinesin lattice binding and MTOC-mediated recruitment/reactivation at minus-ends. Releasing either condition equalizes kinesin distribution and prevents microtubule differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C165-C167 are supported by the combined results from phosphorylation studies (preventing lattice binding) and Bub2/Bfa1 studies (SPB recruitment). The effects of Kip2-S63A and bfa1Δbub2Δ mutations demonstrate the necessity of both conditions. The conclusion is well-supported by multiple lines of evidence.

results.result: Kinesin modification through phosphorylation, rather than microtubule modification, prevents random lattice binding and ensures SPB supremacy in Kip2 recruitment control.
results.evaluation: Claims C169, C170, C174 are supported by the Kip2-S63A mutation studies and the absence of tubulin modifications in yeast (C58). The mechanism is simpler and more direct than tubulin code-based regulation. The conclusion is well-justified by the experimental evidence.

results.result: Kip2 recruitment at SPBs likely requires high-affinity binding sites for phosphorylated Kip2 and local dephosphorylation to release inhibition. An unidentified phosphatase is proposed to activate Kip2 at SPBs.
results.evaluation: Claims C175-C176 are logical inferences based on the need to compete with microtubule binding and to enable motor activity. However, C177 is speculative without direct evidence for phosphatase involvement. The binding sites and dephosphorylation mechanism require experimental validation.

results.result: The authors speculate that the remote-control model may be conserved beyond yeast and could explain tubulin code establishment, with kinesins potentially delivering tubulin modifiers as cargos.
results.evaluation: Claims C178-C180, C183, C185 are speculative proposals without direct experimental support in the manuscript. While C181-C182, C184 cite supporting evidence from other systems, the specific mechanisms proposed require experimental validation. These are reasonable hypotheses for future work.

results.result: Similar asymmetries in aster size and centrosome segregation occur in various organisms, and phosphorylation-regulated kinesins exist in metazoans, suggesting conservation of the messenger kinesin mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C186-C190 are supported by citations to literature on C. elegans, Drosophila, mouse stem cells, and metazoan kinesins. The evidence suggests conservation of key features, though direct demonstration of the complete mechanism in other organisms would strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: Not all kinesins are regulated by MTOCs. Kip3 shows SPB-independent, length-dependent distribution while Kip2 shows SPB-dependent, length-independent distribution, creating a kinesin distribution code that controls microtubule function.
results.evaluation: Claims C191-C196 are supported by the contrasting distribution patterns (Figure 1) and conservation in S. pombe (C194, citation). The concept of a kinesin distribution code is a reasonable synthesis of the findings, though the full complexity of regulation requires further investigation.

results.result: Background knowledge about microtubule structure, function, dynamics, and regulation in eukaryotic cells, including yeast-specific features and kinesin functions.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C65 represent established knowledge supported by appropriate citations to the literature. These provide necessary context for the study but are not novel findings. The citations appear accurate and appropriate.

results.result: Kip2 and Kip3 show different movement patterns in vivo, with Kip2 moving processively at speeds comparable to Kip3, but Kip3 speckles initiating from random positions along microtubules.
results.evaluation: Claims C73, C84, C85 are supported by kymograph analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a, Video 2) and citations to in vitro studies. The contrasting behaviors provide important context for understanding the different regulatory mechanisms.

results.result: Bub2 and Bfa1 function as a GAP complex for Tem1 and are recruited to the old SPB by SPIN, with levels enhanced by proximity to the bud neck. Their distribution pattern resembles that of Kip2.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C122 represent established knowledge about Bub2/Bfa1 supported by appropriate citations. The observation about similarity to Kip2 distribution (C122) is a reasonable inference that motivates the experimental investigation.

results.result: Neither Kip2 phosphorylation nor Bub2/Bfa1 control differential microtubule nucleation rates between m- and b-SPBs, as most preanaphase cells lack measurable m-microtubules in all mutants tested.
results.evaluation: Claim C157 is supported by quantification (Figure 7—figure supplement 1b) showing that m-microtubule formation remains rare in all mutants. This negative result is important for defining the scope of the mechanism.

results.result: Kip2 phosphorylation involves multiple GSK3-targeted sites, which can efficiently maintain high phosphorylation. Preventing phosphorylation does not affect plus-end release rate, indicating phosphorylation specifically prevents lattice reloading.
results.evaluation: Claim C171 is supported by citation. C172 is a reasonable inference about GSK3 mechanism based on established knowledge. C173 is supported by modeling results showing unchanged kout in Kip2-S63A. The conclusions are well-justified.
